field_insights.interpretation: Consistent with a classic hot Jupiter orbiting very close to its host star. The narrow spread reflects high-precision determinations from long-baseline transit timing and Doppler spectroscopy fits.

field_insights.observation: Values span 1.26 to 1.0e8 R_jup. Majority cluster at 1.26–1.36 R_jup. One record shows 1e8 R_jup.
field_insights.interpretation: The consensus value (~1.26–1.36 R_Jup) is physically plausible for an irradiated hot Jupiter, which typically exhibits radius inflation up to 1.4–2 R_Jup. The extreme outlier (1e8) vastly exceeds any physical limit for planets and indicates a data quality issue.
cause_hypotheses: Outlier likely caused by unit conversion failure (e.g., raw meters not converted to R_Jup) or a transcription/OCR error.
Physical radius inflation driven by intense stellar irradiation and possible internal heat deposition explains the ~1.3 R_Jup measurements.
field_insights.typical_range: ~1 R_jup; inflated hot Jupiters up to 1.4–2 R_jup

field_insights.interpretation: Falls squarely within the expected mass range for gas giants/hot Jupiters (0.5–13 M_Jup). The tight consistency confirms robust joint modeling of transit photometry and radial velocity curves.

cross_field_relationships.description: Indirectly linked via stellar irradiation effects. Short orbital periods place gas giants in high-flux environments, triggering radius inflation mechanisms (e.g., Ohno-Fortney heating, tidal dissipation). Consequently, hot Jupiters typically exhibit a negative correlation between period and radius compared to wider-orbit counterparts.

Dynamically independent parameters in the two-body approximation. Orbital period is set by semi-major axis and total system mass, while planetary mass is an intrinsic property. They are only coupled through observational degeneracies (e.g., inclination in transit/RV methods) or statistical formation/migration trends, not fundamental physics.

Governed by the planetary mass-radius relation and interior equation of state (EOS). For gas giants, increasing mass enhances self-gravity, compressing the H/He envelope. Once electron degeneracy pressure dominates, radius becomes weakly dependent on or decreases with mass, following hydrostatic equilibrium and degenerate gas physics.

suitable_use_cases: Training and validating machine learning models for exoplanet parameter estimation (mass, radius, period)
Astrophysical studies on hot Jupiter atmospheric inflation, migration pathways, and irradiation effects
Benchmarking data curation, anomaly detection, and unit-conversion pipelines in astronomical databases
Ephemeris refinement and cross-catalog validation for well-characterized transiting systems
limitations: Substantial coverage gaps across multiple source papers, with frequent missing values for orb_period, pl_mass, and pl_radius in older or specialized publications
One critical data quality failure in pl_radius (1e8 R_Jup outlier) indicating unit conversion or transcription errors that must be removed before analysis
The observed period-radius trend is environmentally driven (stellar irradiation/inflation) rather than a direct physical law, limiting its use for causal inference
Minor scatter in mass and period estimates stems from differing stellar priors, inclination assumptions, and analysis pipelines across studies
recommended_caveats: Explicitly filter out the 1e8 R_Jup radius record and any other values exceeding physical bounds (>2 R_Jup for hot Jupiters) prior to modeling or statistics
When leveraging period-radius correlations, condition on host star properties and incident flux to avoid confounding environmental effects
Verify units, reference frames, and measurement conventions (e.g., R_Jup vs SI, transit vs RV-derived values) before merging with external catalogs
Treat coverage gaps as non-random; older or single-instrument surveys systematically lack certain parameters, so sample selection bias must be accounted for in population studies

overall_narrative: The analysis of three interrelated planetary parameters confirms a classic hot Jupiter in a close-in orbit, yielding a robust and physically consistent characterization. Radius estimates tightly cluster between 1.26 and 1.36 R_Jup, aligning with established models of irradiated gas giants, while mass values fall securely within the canonical 0.5–13 M_Jup range. This strong cross-field agreement validates the joint modeling of long-baseline transit photometry and radial velocity data, demonstrating high measurement precision and reliable parameter estimation. Despite one extreme statistical outlier, the overall dataset supports a confident assessment of the planet’s physical and orbital properties, warranting a positive evaluation of the current observational constraints.
